First listed 2025-12-15 · episode or wrap

Steve Eisman's Masterclass on the 2008 Financial Crisis (Part One) | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 38

Eisman explains the crisis through leverage, deteriorating mortgage quality, concentration of exposures and derivative connections. His strongest analytical lessons are that leverage can masquerade as operating skill, historical loss models can fail when underwriting changes, and like-aged loan vintages reveal deterioration hidden by aggregates. Primary research supports these mechanisms. His account overstates a universal risk-weighting explanation and misdescribes typical subprime introductory rates. Loan-level evidence also complicates his reset-centered causal chain. The blanket claim that real household incomes stopped growing in the early 1990s is contradicted by Census data.

Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.

  • The opening montage repeats later material.
  • Illustrative bank balance sheets expressly omit liquidity and hold ROA constant.
  • He calls 2000 a recession year and gives simplified industry chronology; incidental chronology is not used to judge the investment thesis.
  • The repeated 3% initial subprime rate is load-bearing in the refinancing explanation and is preserved rather than silently corrected.

How he reasons here

  • Decompose ROE into asset profitability and leverage.
  • Treat estimated loan losses as uncertain costs rather than immediately known margins.
  • Question historical risk weights when underwriting changes.
  • Compare loan vintages at equal seasoning and account for tax-refund seasonality.
  • Choose a short instrument with manageable liquidity, borrow costs and capacity.
